To backpedal means to retreat from something you previously said, promised, or committed to — to go back on your own words or decisions, usually because of pressure, criticism, or backlash.

Think of it this way: you moved forward by making a statement or commitment. Now you're moving backward — away from that statement. That reverse movement is backpedaling.

Imagine someone cycling. They pedal forward to move forward. If they pedal backward, the bike slows down or reverses. That physical image maps perfectly onto the figurative meaning: you were moving forward with your words or plans, and now you're reversing them.

In boxing, backpedaling means physically retreating — stepping backward to avoid your opponent. Same energy: you were in a position, and now you're pulling back from it.

This physical picture is worth keeping in your head because it tells you exactly what the word feels like: a retreat, a reversal of direction.

When someone backpedals in real life (not on a bike), they:

  1. Said something, promised something, or took a clear position on something.
  2. Faced criticism, pressure, or unwanted attention because of it.
  3. Are now trying to undo, soften, or distance themselves from what they originally said or decided.

The key word here is retreat. The person is retreating from their own earlier words. They are not simply changing their mind freely — they are pulling back because staying in their original position has become uncomfortable or costly.

Political context:
"The senator said taxes would not go up. After widespread public anger, he backpedaled and said he only meant 'certain types' of taxes."

Here, the senator made a firm statement, got heat for it, and is now trying to walk it back.

Workplace context:
"The manager backpedaled on her promise of a pay raise after the company had a bad quarter."

She made a commitment, circumstances changed (or the pressure was too great), and now she's retreating from it.

Personal context:
"He told his friend the party was 'a terrible idea.' When he saw she was hurt, he backpedaled and said he had just been in a bad mood."

He made a harsh statement, saw the consequences, and started reversing course.

This is important: backpedal carries a slightly negative or critical tone. When you describe someone as backpedaling, you're usually suggesting that:

  • They are being inconsistent.
  • They are caving under pressure rather than standing by their word.
  • Their reversal feels somewhat insincere — like they're only retreating because they got caught or criticized, not because they genuinely changed their mind.

This is what separates backpedaling from simply changing your mind. Changing your mind can be noble and thoughtful. Backpedaling suggests a retreat that's driven by social or political pressure, and it often implies the original statement was what the person really meant.

If a journalist writes "The prime minister backpedaled on her comments," the journalist is suggesting that the reversal is strategic or defensive — not a genuine, principled change of heart.

Backpedaling doesn't always mean completely abandoning what you said. It exists on a spectrum:

Full backpedal: "I never said that." or "I was completely wrong."
Partial backpedal: "I didn't mean it that way," or "I was taken out of context," or "It's more complicated than what I said."

Partial backpedaling is actually more common. The person doesn't fully retreat — they just soften or reframe their original position to reduce the damage. They're trying to preserve some dignity while still distancing themselves from the backlash.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Retract — More formal and direct. "She retracted her statement." This means cleanly withdrawing something said, without necessarily implying pressure or strategic retreat. More neutral.

Walk back — Almost identical to backpedal in casual usage. "The spokesperson walked back the comments." Slightly more neutral, slightly less judgmental.

Flip-flop — Used specifically for people who switch positions repeatedly or for perceived political gain. A flip-flopper keeps changing sides. A backpedaler retreats from one specific thing.

Recant — Very formal, often used in legal or religious contexts. "He recanted his testimony." Means formally and explicitly withdrawing a previous statement.

So: backpedal sits in the casual-to-neutral range, but with a built-in suggestion of pressure-driven retreat.

• She backpedals whenever she gets challenged. (simple present)
  • He backpedaled immediately after the speech. (past tense)
  • They are backpedaling on their earlier announcement. (present continuous)
  • The backpedaling began as soon as the criticism started. (noun form)
To backpedal is to retreat from your own previous words, promises, or positions — usually under pressure — often in a way that feels inconsistent or insincere.
